title: Council Post: AI Will Change The Way Business Leaders Think About Time
text:
Eric Miquelon is President of Avanade North America.
The fact that I’m eating lunch while writing this article tells you something about my relationship with time.
Simply put, I don’t have enough. And I bet you feel the same. No matter who you are or what you do, you could probably use a few more hours in your day.
Why? Maybe it’s because our to-do lists are a mile long. Or maybe it’s because we’re distracted by our digital world’s multitude of pings, chirps and bells.
I’d say it’s a bit of both. But there’s a third factor, and it just might be the most important: When it comes to work, you might spend far too much time on tasks that are neither the most valuable nor the most fulfilling. You’re getting caught up in the little things—looking for meeting notes, trying to find conversation threads to get briefed on the project—you've likely been there.
Cross-Industry Impact
If that doesn’t sound like a big deal, consider the impacts of this on an industry like health care, and in particular, nursing.
Many nurses enter the field because they want to make a human impact and help people. And that’s great! But here’s the thing: While nurses do spend a significant amount of time helping people, they also spend time—a lot of time—doing “documentation.” In fact, according to one study, nurses spend about 35.3% of an average workday entering data and filling out forms. That’s more time than they reported spending on any other aspect of the job. And while documentation is extremely important—critical, even, particularly in health care—it takes up a vast amount of time.
And nurses are not alone. In just about any profession, you’ll find workers spending hours upon hours performing rote tasks—the kind that demands no creativity, no personal touch. These tasks may be essential, but the hours spent on them make businesses less efficient, workers less motivated and products less amazing.
What if, I wonder, we could get those hours back? How much better would our world be?
The Promise Of AI
AI, more than any other recent technology, promises to answer those questions. Already, productivity assistants like Microsoft Copilot are performing tasks that, until recently, could only be accomplished by humans. When thoughtfully integrated into organizations, these technologies could transform our businesses, products, experiences and lives for the better.
I’m thinking about all the marketing teams who crank out Super Bowl Sunday ads. What if, instead of resizing each ad a thousand times, they could simply develop a creative campaign and have AI do the rest? What if AI could not only size and place those ads but also customize them for audiences in real time? I bet advertisers would produce less waste and better creative work.
I'm thinking about legal teams who can use AI to pore over the litany of contracts and documents they receive. In a field where minor wording changes can have big impacts, what if AI could review edits to a contract and help quickly identify the legal ramifications of a change in language?
I’m thinking about the nurse who spends a ton of time inputting data and doing other tasks that don’t involve patient care. What if AI could take those things off their plate? If they had more time to focus on their patients, hospitals would be more efficient, and we’d all be better for it.
What Businesses Can Do
My advice to businesses looking to implement AI in a thoughtful way is simple: Start with people. What do you want people to achieve more of—or do less of—by using AI? Implementing technology for technology's sake is not a sound long-term strategy. Business leaders must take a people-first approach to AI.
Of course, challenges may arise, and challenging conversations may emerge. As AI has become more and more commonplace, it has naturally raised questions on whether it will "replace" certain tasks or even roles within an organization or erase the human touch. So, as business leaders, we need to reposition that. When used responsibly, AI can help us do the higher-level thinking and work that we truly love to do. AI won't make our organizations less human—it has the power to make them more human.
Final Thoughts
AI, when implemented thoughtfully, can free us from the rote and the mundane. That means we can invest more time and energy into what really matters—the exciting, meaningful, creative things we humans do best. AI is already revolutionizing the way we work, and this is only the beginning.
Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have a salad to finish.

title: Council Post: An Outlook On Social Discovery: Trends Transforming How We Connect
text:
KJ Dhaliwal is an accomplished entrepreneur and venture investor. He's currently the CSO of Social Discovery Group and founder of Dil Mil.
In a fast-paced world, the digital and social landscape is ever-evolving, driven by tech advancements and constantly changing user preferences. Social discovery, a concept that centers on the idea of connecting people based on their shared interests and activities, is designed to help people find like-minded individuals for romantic or platonic relationships. As this market is a crossover between dating apps and social media, we estimate the social discovery market to reach nearly $1 billion, which accounts for roughly 10% of the entire online global dating market.
But what is shaping the future of this industry? From AI to avatars, key trends are shaping the way we discover and engage with others in the digital realm.
Virtual Reality And High-Fidelity Avatars
With the increasing accessibility and user-friendliness of VR technology, VR headsets are rapidly gaining popularity, which is leading to a surge in VR-driven social platforms. According to Market.US, in 2022 the VR headset market was $10.1 billion and expected to surge to over $100 billion in 10 years.
This trend is likely to extend to dating apps and social discovery platforms, where the exploration of virtual reality dates is underway thanks to apps such as Flirtual and Nevermet. There are no boundaries anymore with relationships, whether platonic or romantic.
Last year, Dating.com (our portfolio company) hosted the first wedding in the metaverse, something that continues to evolve. Now people can have one-on-one dates or interact with an AI to develop a relationship. As this innovation unfolds, a revolutionary shift in meeting people is imminent, presenting a more convenient and enjoyable alternative to traditional in-person interactions.
With VR worlds comes the evolution of avatars. Where avatars have historically been cartoon characters, technology is transforming the experience. Users are now able to create and design “full-body avatars” that represent who they want to be. From facial and body traits to synthetic voices, avatars will continue to gain momentum and become a standard in many people’s lives.
This alternative avenue for socializing and discovering new connections will mark a significant shift in how people interact and engage with each other.
AI Personalization And Interactions With AI People
Artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping the future of social discovery by analyzing user behavior, preferences and interactions. AI is poised to play an even more significant role in enhancing user experiences.
Looking ahead, AI is expected to take a more active role in facilitating conversations on dating platforms. By suggesting personalized conversation starters based on shared interests, AI can help users break the ice and initiate meaningful interactions, alleviating the initial challenges of connecting with someone and paving the way for an authentic, more profound connection.
Anticipating the future, AI’s role in predicting relationship compatibility is set to become more refined. By analyzing patterns, AI can offer users valuable insights into the dynamics of their relationships, guiding them on how to nurture and sustain worthwhile connections in a way that is authentic to them and ultimately contributing to better-informed choices.
The Niche Community Uprising
As X and Facebook continue to lose users, the era of all-encompassing social networks may be slowly fading away, giving opportunity to specialized, niche communities. This shift is driven by the increasing desire of users to engage with platforms that cater specifically to their unique interests, hobbies and passions. Rather than participating in broad, generic networks, individuals are seeking out communities that provide a more tailored and authentic experience.
With nearly 22% of Americans using online dating services, the market opportunity is great. I see the rise of niche dating and social discovery platforms capitalizing on this because these focus on catering to specific interests or communities. This development aligns with the ongoing user preference for connecting with individuals who share similar passions, emphasizing the importance of finding meaningful connections within a more specialized context.
Niche social discovery dating platforms offer spaces where individuals can bond over shared interests, creating a sense of belonging beyond the generic criteria often used in mainstream dating apps. Whether it’s a shared hobby, a specific cultural background, or a unique interest, these communities are designed to foster deeper connections among like-minded individuals. As a result, users can anticipate a more targeted and enriching dating experience where compatibility is rooted in shared values and passions, leading to the creation of more meaningful and lasting connections.
The future of social discovery is dynamic and exciting, driven by tech innovation. As these trends continue to develop, individuals, businesses and social platforms have the opportunity to capitalize on these advancements to create a more personal and engaging experience for users worldwide.

title: Council Post: The Data Differentiator: Unlocking The Power Of Unstructured Data To Fuel AI
text:
As CEO of Quantum, Jamie is responsible for leading multi-pronged transformation initiatives to drive profitability, growth and innovation.
In the rapidly evolving digital era, unstructured data has become a key player in businesses’ digital transformation journeys. Encompassing a vast array of information forms (from videos and audio clips to images and text), this data type is growing exponentially. For the first time, advanced AI technologies enable us to process, reason and extract meaningful insights from this data, unveiling a world of untapped business opportunities.
A staggering 80% of all data generated is unstructured, such as video surveillance data, images, videos and loT sensor data, which pose both immense potential and significant challenges for organizations looking to catalog and analyze their data. Effectively managing and leveraging this data with AI-powered tools is not just an option but a necessity for businesses aiming to uncover hidden insights and create value.
Recent strides in data storage and AI technology innovation are simplifying key complexities of unstructured data management, allowing organizations to move from merely managing data to turning proprietary unstructured data into a competitive differentiator. Enterprises are increasingly leveraging the newfound ability to generate actionable, data-driven insights from their data. Organizations have to understand the dynamic world of unstructured data, its management challenges, and how new AI capabilities can help simplify managing and enriching this data.
The Unstructured Data Landscape
Organizations today have millions or even billions of files, but their traditional storage systems are confined to storing file names without insight into the actual content of that file. This lack of context is the challenge in keeping unprecedentedly high volumes of unstructured data that companies want to retain for insights and analysis.
How do you make sense of that much information when you can’t even discern what exactly it is or what purpose it might eventually serve? How do you know what’s happening in every clip of that video surveillance footage, for example? Is there a slip and fall? Did someone get injured?
Traditionally, it would require hundreds of hours of human resources to manually search through every video clip to find that data. With AI, however, the organization can automatically tag, annotate, catalog and organize the data—making it easily searchable, accessible and, ultimately, usable in a new way.
Data enrichment should be in the very DNA of the storage architecture. By infusing AI capabilities into the core of data storage, organizations empower their unstructured data to contribute to business insights and outcomes actively.
AI Differentiation Using Your Data
AI models require massive amounts of data from which to learn. Most organizations are using readily available data on the internet to fuel and train their AI models. However, what sets you apart from every other organization in the data-driven arena and gives you a differentiated advantage is your unique data—things like your organization’s support calls, training videos, research data, video surveillance footage and more.
It is exclusively shielded from the homogeneity of generic datasets that others can access. It is a tailored asset inherently aligned with the intricacies of your operations. This level of customization ensures that every piece of information extracted is relevant and essential to giving your organization a critical competitive advantage. Organizations that have archived and retained all of their unstructured data will have a distinct advantage over those that have “thrown theirs away.”
The rise of AI and unstructured data—and, therefore, the value contained in that data—has shifted how organizations think about their storage and infrastructure. An end-to-end strategy is essential because extracting value is about navigating the entire life cycle of unstructured data, from creation to enrichment and analysis to archival, ensuring that AI intelligence is embedded at every step.
To begin this journey toward implementing an AI-based data strategy, there are several steps organizations should take to future-proof their organizations.
It begins with a thorough evaluation of existing data assets, with a focus on assessing their quality, accessibility and relevance. Clear goal-setting aligned with specific business objectives—complemented by establishing measurable key performance indicators (KPIs)—serves as a cornerstone for success. On the technology side, establishing an AI model evaluation process as early as possible is a challenging but critical step.
Another important aspect is standardizing data collection, storage and management processes with an emphasis on automation, which ensures consistency and reliability and must be maintained from the beginning of the AI initiative.
Simultaneously, the development of robust data governance policies addresses critical concerns surrounding privacy, security and compliance. The capabilities of AI technology are growing exponentially, and staying at the forefront of it is not negotiable. For example, emerging methodologies such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can effectively harness internal expertise while mitigating potential challenges such as hallucination and keeping the proprietary data secure.
More than ever, the success or failure of fast-moving AI projects hinges on two main factors: the team and the culture. When we encourage a culture where trying new things and sharing knowledge is valued, it helps us work together better and get better results. It’s important to keep investing in training our teams so they understand data and AI better. This helps everyone stay on the same page and keep improving fast.
Unstructured data, once an overlooked aspect of data management, has now become a cornerstone in the AI-driven business landscape. The organizations that will thrive are those that recognize the intrinsic value of their unique data and leverage AI to transform this data into actionable insights. As we look ahead, the ability to manage, enrich and use unstructured data will not just be a competitive differentiator but a fundamental criterion for success in the digital age.

title: AI comes to the world of beauty as eyelash robot uses artificial intelligence to place fake lashes
text:
AI comes to the world of beauty as eyelash robot uses artificial intelligence to place fake lashes
Luum's AI can place eyelid extensions faster than a human, but expert urges caution
Artificial intelligence is making its way into esthetics with a new application in eyelash extensions.
A Bay Area-based company called Luum has released an AI-powered eyelash extension machine, currently available at only a few select California locations.
Nathan Harding, CEO and co-founder of Luum, who is based in Oakland, California, told Fox News Digital in an interview that the company is using robotics and AI to "completely transform the experience of eyelash extensions."
WHAT IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE?
"For the client, it's going to be super fast, super comfortable and super consistent," he said.
"And the provider will be able to do three times the appointments they could do otherwise."
Salon owners and lash technicians will be able to "concentrate on the artistry part of it," rather than the "backbreaking, tedious labor," Harding said.
A typical Luum appointment starts with choosing lash length, density, volume and shape, president Jo Lawson told Fox News Digital in the same interview.
GOOGLE BARD TRANSITIONS TO GEMINI: WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE AI UPGRADE
After separating the client’s lashes, the lash artist will position the client in a "super comfortable chair" and slide the person into the Luum machine.
"Your eyes are taped closed, and they slide you in, position you correctly [and] set the machine to do the job," Lawson said.
The machine typically places 50 to 60 lashes on each eye unless the client has requested more density during a consultation.
Once Luum is finished with the placement, the lash artist will touch up the robot’s work by manually adding a few lashes at the end.
A full set of lashes via Luum takes about an hour and 15 minutes to complete, while a refill takes about 50 minutes — about 30% faster than it would if a human had placed them.
HEAD OF GOOGLE BARD BELIEVES AI CAN HELP IMPROVE COMMUNICATION AND COMPASSION: ‘REALLY REMARKABLE’
The beauty store Ulta currently charges $170 for a full Luum set and $80 for a refill, comparatively cheaper than other extension services.
Luum right now has one machine running at Ulta’s South San Jose location, where it is "almost completely booked every single day," according to Lawson.
The company's goal is to have Luum machines at every Ulta in the country.
Luum is currently working on an advanced machine that will work four times faster than a human, Harding pointed out.
The upgraded machine will address both eyes at the same time, as the current model does one eye at a time, Lawson added.
How the AI works
Lawson described the Luum lash machine as a "fun thing" to experience, even for people who aren't tech-savvy.
"There's nobody leaning on your forehead with these super sharp instruments, literally a millimeter from your eyeball," he said.
"So, it just feels safer, it feels cleaner, it's faster and the clients are loving it."
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE EXPERTS SHARE 6 OF THE BIGGEST AI INNOVATIONS OF 2023: 'A LANDMARK YEAR'
While it might seem that having a robot so close to the eye could be dangerous, Harding said it's "purely mechanical."
"The only thing that [the machine] could physically reach you with are these little featherweight tools," he said.
"We need to know where your upper eyelid is very accurately, and neural networks do those kinds of tasks fantastically."
"And we engineer those tools so that, unlike in the human process, they have very springy little tips, and then we also attach those tools to the robot."
Luum incorporates the "old-school classical techniques" of computer vision, which are still "very sophisticated" but not to the level of modern-day machine learning, and then combines it with artificial intelligence technology, according to Harding.
"And then we use the machine … to create a lot of data, tons and tons of images, and then we can use those images to train neural networks to do certain things … like finding the edge of your upper eyelid," he said.
"We need to know where your upper eyelid is very accurately, and neural networks do those kinds of tasks fantastically."
AI DEFINES ‘IDEAL BODY TYPE’ PER SOCIAL MEDIA – HERE'S WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE
The neural networks can tell the machine whether it’s in good orientation with the eyelid before honing in on a target lash, he said.
"The neural network will make the decision on the best place to put this little probe the next time so that it's most likely to isolate a lash," said Harding.
Future of AI and beauty
Luum is patented in 48 countries, with customers already pre-ordering the machines for their salons.
The machine is currently sold to a salon for $129,000, with $62,000 of that going toward shipping, installation and training, according to the company.
CHATGPT LIFE HACKS: HOW USERS ARE SPAWNING GROCERY LISTS FROM AI-GENERATED RECIPES AND MEAL PLANS
"It's in our best interest to make sure that we cue our customers up, get them trained well and have them in a situation where they're making money while we're making money," Lawson said.
"This machine only gets more valuable over time."
"[Technicians] can raise their productivity greatly – and that means there's going to be greater income for them, and also that the physically demanding jobs are going to get easier."
TEENS ARE TURNING TO SNAPCHAT'S 'MY AI' FOR MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT — WHICH DOCTORS WARN AGAINST
This kind of AI application eventually could extend into other services, such as hair removal, semi-permanent tattooing of eyebrows, spray tanning, tattooing and makeup, Harding said.
Finding a robot that can leverage AI and learn over time is "really where the value is," according to Lawson.
Harding responded that it's "exactly the kind of robot application I love, where you're not replacing someone."
He added, "You're taking a very valuable, high-revenue, high-margin person, and you're [tripling] the revenue they can do. That's where robotics really makes huge leaps."
Potential risks and limitations
Harvey Castro, an emergency medicine physician in Coppell, Texas, is also a consultant and speaker on AI and ChatGPT in health care.
He's not affiliated with Luum but offered his input on potential safety concerns and considerations.

"The device's proximity to the sensitive eye area could raise concerns about the risk of eye infections or allergic reactions to the materials used in the lash extensions," Castro told Fox News Digital.
"Ensuring that the system can maintain a sterile environment and that the materials used are hypoallergenic and safe for close contact with the eye area is crucial."
While robotics and computer vision promise high precision, he noted, there's always a concern about the margin of error — "especially in a procedure as delicate as lash extensions, where slight misplacements could lead to discomfort or injury."
"Thorough evaluation and transparency regarding safety, efficacy and regulatory compliance are essential."
Training and oversight of technicians is another area of concern, Castro noted.
"Ensuring that operators are well-versed in both the technology and emergency procedures in case of malfunction or adverse reactions is essential for client safety," he said.

title: Refik Anadol’s New Show At Serpentine London Is A Love Letter To Nature
text:
In the heart of London’s lively Kensington Gardens, embedded in the city’s nature, Serpentine Galleries (North) is hosting "Echoes of the Earth: Living Archive" from February 16th to April 7th, 2024. A must see exhibition that merges artificial intelligence with nature’s beauty, through the innovative lens of Refik Anadol. Known for his pioneering work in AI art, this show demonstrates Anadol’s expertise in bringing digital art uniquely to life, presenting a series of works that redefine our interaction with AI and give us new perspectives on the depths of nature and human connection.
The exhibition features dynamic interpretations of natural landscapes, including underwater scenes and rainforests, through the most advanced AI technology. A key work, "Artificial Realities: Coral (2023)," immerses you in a digitally crafted oceanic space, using a dataset of over 135 million coral images to create a stunning visual experience.
Another highlight is the "Living Archive: Large Nature Model," making its (remastered) UK debut, after premiering at the World Economic Forum in Davos earlier this year, where I’ve learned about it first. This installation showcases an AI that interprets the natural world. Joseph Fowler, Head of Arts & Culture at the World Economic Forum who commissioned both these artworks for the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meetings in Davos (Artificial Realities: Coral, 2023 and Dataland: Rainforest, 2024 - both are nature driven artworks of purpose) explains the connection and his work with Anadol:
“Art has the power and the potential to ignite change on both individual and societal levels, making it a powerful force for positive transformation in the world. As technology is more and more present within our everyday lives, I wanted to explore the concept of what it means to be human in the age of machine intelligence as perceived through an arts lens.” Fowler continues: “One of the challenges we face today is the disconnect we often feel from global issues and the problems faced by others. As important as data is, it can lead to feelings of overwhelm and disassociation rather than empowerment and engagement. By engaging with a work by Refik Anadol, you are given a unique opportunity and new way to visualise and comprehend data in immersive and interactive artworks that connects your senses, body, and mind.”
Anadol expresses his excitement over this project, viewing it as a milestone in AI art: “This show is the very first time we are using our Large Nature Model research. Since last year we have been partnering with incredible technology leaders, museums, archives, genius researchers and scientists who have been preserving nature across the world. In ‘Echoes of the Earth’, almost five years of nature research and a year of developing the Large Nature Model are coming alive. We are showcasing our early studies on the flora, fauna and landscapes of the rainforest coupled with our coral research, combining them with image, sound, text and scent. The scents showcased in the exhibition are also specially created for Serpentine.”
Anadol's work, offers a new perspective on digital impressions that shape our lives. He challenges viewers to consider technology's influence on our perception of nature, time, space, and humanity's place in an AI-driven world. During our conversation he shares what inspired his environmental work: “I met with the Yanawana family who are an incredible indigenous culture and tribe living in Amazonia in Brazil Acre, two years ago. It was through them that I learned how they are living in harmony with nature and how they are so important to the protection and preservation of the rainforest. Moments like these brought a realization that all of the projects our studio takes on have to focus on nature in the hopes of creating context, discourse, and attention.” Soon after, Chief Nixiwaka of the Ywanawa family became Anadol’s mentor. His words to Anadol sound sound like “messages to humanity through the lens, through the eyes, through the perspective of nature.” which Anadol perfectly understands to implement into his visual works.
“Chief Nixiwaka is an extremely important role model for me as a human. He is one of the most important indigenous leaders of the Amazonia who was able to protect his language and his culture.” Anadol adds.
“Our recent nature-focused AI works are a kind of love letter to Nature. I think we have a simple human instinct and reflex; we do not hurt something we love.” (Refik Anadol)
He also shares a quote by his mentor, that he holds close to his heart: “It is new times we are living now. Time for forgiveness. Time for love. Time for spirituality. It is time for humanity to look back to the origins. To the Earth. To our hearts. To learn, to love and respect one another. To make alliances, join forces. This is the moment.” (Chief Nixiwaka).
Serpentine's leadership, including CEO Bettina Korek and Artistic Director Hans Ulrich Obrist, not only supports Anadol's vision but deeply aligns with it. They see the exhibition as an intersection of art, science, and technology, aiming to captivate but also to educate viewers. This initiative is part of Serpentine's broader exploration of AI's role in art, emphasizing the gallery's commitment to innovation. The entry to the galleries and to this show is free, symbolizing a welcoming invitation to anyone curious to explore
Part of Serpentine's New Alliances program, the exhibition underscores the gallery's role in promoting digital-age art. Serpentine’s engagement with AI, including establishing the Creative AI Lab, highlights its leadership in discussions on technology's cultural impact. Its commitment to free access ensures the exhibition reaches a wide audience, furthering the dialogue on art and technology's evolving relationship.

title: How Students Can ‘Future-Proof’ Themselves As AI Disrupts The Workforce
text:
As artificial intelligence transforms the economy, students need to “future-proof” themselves, educators warn.
Exactly how jobs and professions will change is not yet clear, but universities tasked with producing employable graduates are already thinking about how higher education can stay relevant amid the uncertainty.
“We are in the difficult position of not fully knowing what the concrete outcomes of AI’s impact will be,” says University of Tokyo President Teruo Fujii. “But we are at the same time responsible for educating students to enter a society that will essentially be reinvented by this advanced technology,” he adds.
Fujii was recently in New York for an AI symposium and moderated a panel discussion last month at AI House Davos, held in conjunction with the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting.
He says students who are entering university during this period of flux can “future-proof” themselves by choosing certain academic pathways and participating in internships and real world experiences that will test what they’ve learned in the classroom.
In the past, as auto assembly line workers or toll booth collectors were eliminated by automation, the focus was on how to retrain blue-collar workers. But because artificial intelligence can seemingly perform cognitive tasks, the technology may replace some white-collar jobs in fields traditionally pursued by university graduates.
From language translation and text summarization to logical reasoning and predictive analysis, AI has the capacity to replace jobs in fields such as financial analysis, research and data analytics, and content creation.
Here are some tips from President Fujii for students to prepare for this new era:
Embrace interdisciplinary study as a new foundation for a university education
Being a specialist in one academic area may not be encompassing enough to tackle many of today’s complex challenges, such as those contending with climate change and infectious diseases. Students should be encouraged to be more interdisciplinary, exploring diverse disciplines and combining their strengths, such as humanities and social sciences with STEM fields, says Fujii.
For example, University of Tokyo’s “SPRING GX” program allows doctoral students from any of its schools to study humanities, business management, engineering, science and medicine to address the complex social challenges of “green transformation,” as industry focuses on generating growth while safeguarding resources.
Interdisciplinary study will also help foster skills that are unique to human beings, such as creativity and critical thinking, that will become even more valuable in a technologically advanced world.
“Students are developing their own expertise, but at the same time they could gain core knowledge about important, common issues,” Fujii adds. “These literacies should be integrated with a sound understanding of technology and data.”
Pursue “real life” experiences that put knowledge to the test
In a tech-driven world, real-life experiences become more valuable. Students need to know what machines can do but also discover what sets them apart — what they can do that machines cannot. They must integrate the classroom experience with real world experience, the university president said.
These experiences allow students to assess their competence and identify areas for improvement. The University of Tokyo provides hands-on learning opportunities in diverse settings, fostering empathy and global business experience, from remote villages to overseas corporate branches. Experience-based learning reveals knowledge gaps, encouraging students to address them. Unlike machines, Fujii says, students translate knowledge into new contexts, take risks, and learn that failure is part of the process.
Keep learning, post-graduation, as skills demands evolve
As AI and technology transform the workplace, there's a shared responsibility to avoid leaving anyone behind. The main challenge is to establish effective measures for continuous reskilling and upskilling, providing individuals with the tools to navigate a rapidly changing job market.
In this ongoing process, the potential for new technology or startup opportunities remains significant when students think about their careers. Consequently, educators' responsibilities extend beyond initial job placement or further study. Higher education must guide individuals throughout their careers, ensuring ongoing learning to maintain relevant and productive skills, Fujii says.
Some countries will have challenges that are unique to a given society. In a country like Japan, where education has traditionally focused on memorizing knowledge, the integration of AI into higher education may accelerate the need to shift how students learn. Fujii argues that, “the emphasis will now be on adapting to change.”
“The AI landscape is vast,” he says, and “is not limited to language models like GPT-4.”
This necessitates a new way of thinking about higher education in Japan. Under Fujii’s vision, the University of Tokyo is planning to create an entirely new college centered around a curriculum to nurture more autonomous, entrepreneurial and resilient individuals with a strong sense of social commitment to design within a rapidly-changing society.
As universities across the globe begin to integrate artificial intelligence into their curriculums, students may actually be more adept at the advanced technology than their professors.
“There may be a shift in the changing dynamics of education,” says Fujii. “Students may know more than their professors, highlighting a shift in the traditional roles within academia.”

title: Is AI Biased - Does It Help Or Hinder Women As They Rise To The Top?
text:
For the past four years, the research team behind InnovateHERs has been peeling back layers from the data to understand better how and why women become successful in purpose-driven sectors.
We’ve seen firsthand the unique strengths women must develop throughout their careers to rise to the top, and we continuously see that they are drawn to creating a positive impact in their work. As we’ve built on this research, we’ve also seen that many of the skills and traits women possess are a direct response to the biases, stereotypes, and roadblocks that face them as they grow in their professional areas. Simply put, women must overcome many barriers in a world often tilted against them to reach the C-Suite.
With the proliferation of AI tools hitting the market over the past year, it was almost impossible not to wonder if the same biases we saw reflected in our research might be built into these tools and the large language models (LLM) driving AI.
When I began writing this blog, I began by trying out prompts to see what ChatGPT would return. Of course, the research team was curious (and slightly skeptical) about what our controversial subject would say about themselves. It’s like the saying in journalism: always get a quote from your subject. AI was the 'subject' in this case, and we wanted to hear what it had to say.
Our starting point was a classic AI experiment, employing ChatGPT to unravel the stereotypes embedded in the LLMs that comprise AI tools. We started with a simple analogy and allowed ChatGPT to fill in the blanks: "Father is to Doctor as Mother is to…" The AI's response, "Nurse," was telling. Reversing the roles to "Mother is to Doctor as Father is to…" yielded a more neutral, yet equally revealing answer: “The analogy "mother is to doctor as father is to '' suggests a parallel relationship. In this case, the logical completion could be "father is to engineer" or any other profession typically associated with a person's occupation.
A sharp inhale. Maybe it’s just that one platform—we should try another.
As the investigation is almost exclusively focused on purpose-driven sectors, we continued to investigate the healthcare theme. Using the ubiquitous presentation platform Canva, we began to generate images using the platform’s proprietary Magic Media tool. A quick image creation prompt for “nurse” was predictably disappointing as we saw the biases that women have worked so hard to refute appear on our screens. Pictures of scantily dressed young women with a small Red Cross somewhere on the image were prolific. A follow-up search for “Doctor” included the majority of images as older, distinguished white men with glasses on, staring condescendingly back at us.
It’s not shocking, but it is enough to make you want to slam your laptop shut curl up in bed with a good book, and forget the internet ever existed. But now is not the time to look away.
Facing a reality where only 26% of employees in AI and machine-learning companies are women, and less than 19% of AI researchers identify as women, the urgency to intensify our efforts toward diversifying the leadership in technology startups—particularly those driven by AI—has never been more critical. If we are to ensure that these biases do not become even more hard-coded into our society and perpetuated as the pace of innovation continues to accelerate, we must act now.
There is another reason we believe women must lead AI companies. In the research from InnovateHERs: Why Purpose-Driven Entrepreneurial Women Rise to the Top, it’s become clear that when women lead organizations, they lead with great heart and compassion for their customers and users. Instead of the lack of empathy, we are witnessing as the tech giants were put on trial in Congress over the past few weeks, our research revealed that women are more inclined to use their unique skills and traits not only to mitigate the risks AI might pose to users, but to leverage this technology for the good of humankind.
A simple place to begin is highlighting the women who are already leading AI-driven startups and looking at how they are leveraging it for good.
There is Reshma Saujani, the founder of Girls Who Code and now Moms First, which launched a tool called Paid Leave AI that uses AI to help women and parents across the country understand their paternity leave policies and rights as parents.
Emily Oster, the economist, professor, and author of Expecting Better: Why the Conventional Pregnancy Wisdom Is Wrong–and What You Really Need to Know, is also supporting new mothers by launching a tool called ParentData, which unpacks data-driven decisions around pregnancy, motherhood, and childcare.
From our research, we spotlight Dr. Patricia Scanlon, founder, and former CEO of Soapbox Labs. This company applies AI to develop speech recognition applications that are specifically tuned to children's voices. Inspired by watching her daughter use educational apps on her iPad, Dr. Scanlon developed voice recognition technology that aimed to improve early literacy.
If you have followed the OpenAI story over the past year, you will have heard of Mira Murati who leads the AI development at OpenAI. She is a strong advocate for regulating AI and public testing of AI technology. Her passion for AI, combined with her open-mindedness, has solidified her as one of the most influential women in tech today. We believe she will be mindful of the biases in AI and work diligently to correct this.
In a blue ocean market, we know that there is a world of opportunity. Now more than ever, the time to include and promote women into top leadership positions is urgent. With women leading the charge, our research suggests we will see less structural biases hard coded into AI applications and less bias in the new and updated LLM, and hopefully, more AI tools that are helping to create positive global change.
Special thanks to Laura Smulian, researcher, and writer, for her contributions to this piece and to InnovateHERs: Why Purpose-Driven Women Rise to the Top.
Follow me on Twitter or LinkedIn. Check out my website or some of my other work here.

title: Council Post: The Top 4 Trends That HR Leaders Should Embrace In 2024
text:
Eva Majercsik is the Chief People Officer for Genesys, a global leader in customer experience orchestration.
The past few years have brought many challenges and new strategies for HR departments. We've really seen this with the rise of AI implementation and the continued evolution of the workplace. I don’t see the innovations and changes within the workplace slowing down in 2024.
Here are some key trends I'm anticipating for the year.
1. The 'Boomer-ang' Era
According to the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL), the number of people aged 65 and older working or seeking work has increased by 144% in the past 20 years, and 68% of people who retired during the pandemic would consider returning to work. There are many different reasons that this “Boomer-ang” phenomenon is happening.
The past few years have seen quite a shift across the workforce spectrum—from the work week, working environments and a changing economy—which has caused many people to reconsider their views on career plans. The mentality that many retirees had was one of a hustle culture, which primarily focused on ensuring their careers were thriving and left limited time for activity outside of work. Without jobs to fill most of their day, many adults in this population struggle to occupy their time and socialize. Because a sense of purpose is one of the most valuable motivators for people to get out of bed each day, a new role in the workforce is one way to fill this need.
Another reason a retiree would “boomerang” back to work is the current economic state. A study by F&G Annuities & Life found that inflation has negatively impacted retirees’ savings, and they don’t want to solely rely on the income from a pension or Social Security. By returning to work, they can have additional funds for more financial freedom.
No matter the reason a person comes back to the workforce, as an HR professional, we must ensure we create an inclusive culture, especially considering the unique opportunities and challenges of a more hybrid workforce. With most retirees feeling judged by co-workers because of their age, it's extremely important to create an environment where employees are empathetic and support each other to ensure that everyone is successful.
2. Further Adoption Of AI
In 2023, we saw AI become a star. While it's been used in the HR workplace for decades, this technology was thrust into the spotlight last year as a tool to support many different tasks. It seemed to be the only thing people were talking about, and I don’t see that slowing down anytime soon. In fact, in a recent Gartner benchmarking session, 52% of HR leaders said "they were exploring potential use cases and opportunities when it came to generative AI."
While there are many wonderful uses for AI in HR, integrating it successfully relies on ensuring past biases aren’t carried through. One example of this is after AI creates a job posting, someone from HR goes through to make sure the language used is inclusive and doesn’t limit people from applying. Incorporating AI also requires using it as a tool to support—not replace—humans. For instance, AI support can do the vetting during the initial recruitment process, but a professional should make the final decision. After all, if you let AI take over too much of the application vetting process, you may miss out on aspects like cultural fit, transferable skills and other important contexts that a human would be able to recognize.
3. Continued Debate On The Return To Office
Along with AI being a hot topic, the return-to-office conversation will continue to be top of mind in 2024. We were already seeing many companies mandating that employees return to the office a few days a week in 2023. Now, many of those companies are bumping their mandates to four or five days a week.
It's important for businesses to take a step back to understand whether employees are truly happy about the return to office and make pivots based on feedback. Listening to employee feedback will help build trust and ensure valuable talent stays at the company.
4. A Force For Good
My final prediction for 2024 is that HR will mobilize an evolution to ensure companies are using their products and services for good. With everything happening in the world, people expect businesses to actively align with their values and support causes that have positive impacts. Companies need to look at how they empower their workforce to support organizations on both a local and global scale; otherwise, they may lose the loyalty of both their customers and their employees.
At my company, Genesys, our culture is one where making a positive impact is embedded in all we do. It's more than just giving financially or volunteering. It's at the core of how we approach our business. In 2021, we committed to a goal of touching more than 100 million lives by 2030 by using our technology for good. As a part of reaching that goal, we aid nonprofits like the Canadian Red Cross, National Domestic Violence Hotline and Lighthouse Works by shining a light on how their organizations are impacting communities and people for the better.
Conclusion
The HR office has seen a dramatic shift over the past few years, and we shouldn’t anticipate it settling down any time soon. Between new innovations and the need to tailor workforce strategies to employees' expectations, HR can't afford to be stagnant. Agile, flexible strategies will drastically improve the employee experience, in turn allowing organizations to attract and retain the best talent and, ultimately, gain a competitive edge.

title: Council Post: Accelerating Product Development For The AI Age
text:
Tyler serves as Broadridge's Chief Technology and Product Officer, responsible for global tech innovation.
The sudden emergence of ChatGPT in 2022 kicked off a race to create new products powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI). Now, companies in all industries are trying to build the ability to develop and come to market with AI-driven products.
When ChatGPT was launched, my colleagues and I at Broadridge joined our peers at other firms in feeling both excitement and pressure to deliver commercial solutions utilizing the new technology. In June 2023, we rolled out BondGPT, an AI platform for corporate bond trading that was developed and delivered in 12 weeks.
Whenever I'm asked for advice about how other companies can turn around new AI products at a similar speed, I give the same answer: You probably can't unless you've already spent time building the operational foundation needed to develop products at that pace.
While it's technically correct to say we built BondGPT in 12 weeks, the reality is that we had been working for years to find the right processes to accelerate our product development. We understood that innovation was speeding up, and we knew we had to speed up as well. The model we used to accomplish that goal could hold valuable lessons for other companies working to build a product development capability for the new age of AI.
Adopt A Product-Based Operating Model
Creating a product development process that can deliver an AI-powered product in the span of weeks takes an organization-wide commitment. Companies should start at the highest level by rethinking their operational model.
At Broadridge, 80% of our organization is structured around small, autonomous and integrated teams. Each team has complete ownership of a distinct product or platform. Each of these products and platforms is, in turn, embedded within an end-to-end client solution. Adopting this type of product-based operating model makes it easier for companies to prioritize work, allocate resources, establish leadership, and ensure that goals cascade and link at all levels of the organization.
Cultivate Delivery Excellence
The ability to deliver products quickly is a skill that must be cultivated over time. It begins with the process: To work effectively at this pace, companies need to "shift left" by moving security and testing to the start of the development process and then automate testing and operations wherever possible. Companies will also have to incorporate elements of agile strategy to maintain value assurance and create an iterative design process that responds to evolving technology and customer needs.
Next comes the right technology. To accelerate the process and ensure the company keeps pace with rivals as well as client expectations, companies must continually adopt the latest engineering tooling, infrastructure and practices. We've found that upgrading these capabilities can make developers more than three times as productive.
Emphasize The Architecture
The speed and effectiveness of any product development effort is a direct function of the technology architecture that supports it. The best foundation is a simple, reusable, microservices-based architecture combined with a scalable technical stack capable of evolving over time as technology and business requirements change.
The design process for this architecture is in many ways as important as the architecture itself. Decision-making about architecture should be viewed less as a governance function and more as a practical part of the development process. We are involving functions from cyber to legal as early in the design process as possible, as AI makes data security and privacy central issues.
Devote Resources To Data
Data is a primary constraint on AI product development. In financial services and other businesses, there is no room for phantom answers; the first answer must be the correct answer. In that environment, companies must be sure that the data they are feeding into large language models (LLMs) is accurate, robust and, in many cases, real time.
We've devoted huge amounts of time and resources to implementing a data ontology that meets both general business needs and the specific requirements of AI. For the latter, we are housing all of our data in defined "neighborhoods" in which we can allow or prohibit access to LLMs. We're also establishing procedures to determine which data can be used externally and which will live behind the firewall. Throughout this process, data experts and technologists coordinate closely with legal teams to ensure data security and privacy.
Encourage Innovation
In my experience, the best way to generate good ideas for new AI applications is to get the technology into the hands of professionals as quickly as possible. We've established an environment where all employees can have access to ChatGPT. This system allows our people to learn how the technology works, test its capabilities and experiment with new ideas.
It's still early days for this project, but the flywheel is starting to spin. We have business users coming in with great ideas. The strongest concepts often come from domain experts who are in the best position to spot opportunities for the technology to meet real business needs. That's exactly what happened with BondGPT.
We have proprietary data on trading techniques and patterns from the dealers and clients who use our networks. It was our fixed-income domain experts who spotted the opportunity to harvest that rich IP to create real benefits for traders by getting critical information into their hands faster and with much less effort.
Ideas like these should fuel a steady stream of pilot initiatives designed to create use cases and assess the viability of concepts. Our pilot for BondGPT proved that by applying a generative AI solution to our proprietary network data, we could reduce the time it takes for traders to research bonds and execute trades from more than 20 minutes to just a few minutes.
With a proven viable concept, we kicked off the development process that delivered BondGPT in 12 weeks. However, for companies looking to replicate that performance, the most important lesson from this story is that the work that enabled that turnaround didn't start in 2022 or 2023—it's been going on for years.

title: Will AI Replace Consultants? Here’s What Business Owners Say.
text:
Of all the professions in the world of business, consultants get a bad rap. They go in, survey the scene and make their recommendations. Whether or not their advice turns into growth, the consultant still gets paid. Some charge thousands a day, others take equity for good measure. Some are great and some need work.
The rise of artificial intelligence tools in business throughout 2023 and beyond has started a debate as to which roles will remain and which will be replaced. Coaches might be safe but lawyers might not. Admin assistants, call center workers, each job function requires a rethink. In this series of assessments by entrepreneurs, AI experts and consultants, consultants themselves are under scrutiny. Here’s what other professionals think will happen to these day rate strategists.
Can artificial intelligence replace consultants? The debate.
Yes, AI will replace consultants
“Most consultants aren’t actually that smart," said Michael Greenberg of Modern Industrialists. “They’re just smarter than the average person.” But he reckons the average machine is much smarter. “Consultants generally do non-creative tasks based around systematic analysis, which is yet another thing machines are normally better at than humans.” Greenberg believes some consultants, “doing design or user experience, will survive,” but “the run of the mill accounting degree turned business advisor will not.”
Someone who has “replaced all of [her] consultants with ChatGPT already, and experienced faster growth,” is Isabella Bedoya, founder of MarketingPros.ai. However, she thinks because “most people don't know how to use AI, savvy consultants need to leverage it to become even more powerful, effective and efficient for their clients” and stay ahead of their game. Heather Murray, director at Beesting Digital, thinks the inevitable replacement of consultants is down to quality. “There are so many poor quality consultants that rely rigidly on working their clients through set frameworks, regardless of the individual’s needs. AI could do that easily.” She agrees “the high quality consultants will prevail, but they’ll only stay competitive by arming themselves with AI.”
AI business consultant Damien Sebastian thinks it’s a matter of timing. “In the short to medium term, a lot of consultants will be put out of a job,” and he has a theory on why. “The demand for consultancy work is growing, but this growth is matched by how AI technology is speeding up common tasks such as writing reports and analysis,” an imbalance he thinks “will result in job losses, because fewer consultants are needed to do the same amount of work.” Similar to Murray, Sebastian believes, “high performing consultants will use AI tools as co-pilots, increasing their outputs exponentially, while big consulting companies will become infinitely more lean and profitable.”
Rob Da Costa, who helps agency owners make their agency less dependent on them, with 1-to-1 coaching and AskRobAnythingAI, believes, “AI-powered virtual assistants could handle many routine consulting tasks like gathering basic client information, explaining processes and options, providing recommendations based on parameters, and answering common questions,” a process he believes would replace many consultants while also being positive for their human counterpart. “This would allow human consultants to focus on higher-level strategic work and develop personal relationships,” along with their “depth of understanding, empathy, and the ability to read between the lines, understand the nuances of human emotion and behaviour, and offer tailored advice based on years of experience and intuition.”
Tim Glowa has worked in HR consulting, including partner level, at global HR, tax and accounting firms. Leading a human capital analytics solution, involving employee surveys, he believes, “the generation of questions, programming a survey, sending out email invitations, analyzing data, writing a report, can easily be replaced with AI,” as well as communication and some tax functions. Other areas, including strategy, pricing and auditing, he thinks will follow suit, but not yet, because they “still require thought and experience and AI isn't at that level.” Glowa thinks AI can level the playing field between large and small consultancy firms. “We were worried about boutique specialized consultancies that can do something of equal quality faster and cheaper,” by leveraging AI. “At least I hope they can!” he added.
No, AI will not replace consultants
“Good consultants bring the human experience and context-driven guidance that AIs aren't able to do,” said Heather Flanagan of Spherical Cow Consulting. She believes, “AI is a fantastic value-add, as it can help a consultant scale engagements and lead generation.” As a consultant herself, she thinks “it's a value add more to us than to what we offer to our clients.” Joffrey Berti, rapid transformational coach and strategy consultant, also believes human experience matters too much to be replaced by robots. "AI lacks the human consultant's ability to understand nuanced business contexts and the complex dynamics of organizational culture. Human consultants bring a level of creativity and strategic insight informed by years of experience and personal judgment that AI cannot replicate yet especially on complex multidimensional projects.”
For Chantal Swainston, founder of The Heard, situational experience is just too important. “The best consultants rely on their experiences to give the best advice,” she said. “Having access to someone who has been in your very specific situation before, managed the process and the results, and can spot the less obvious pitfalls is invaluable.” She said she can see AI “providing a significant amount of assistance, and accelerating people the first few steps before speaking to a consultant, but replacing them completely feels unlikely to me.”
Founder of Mashman Venture Isaac Mashman also believes the demand won’t be there. “Sure, AI can give general answers and be trained on a case-by-case basis, but to imagine people will adopt at scale is unlikely. Humans present a degree of connection AI does not have,” he added.
Senior strategist Jim Perry thinks predictability and emotional intelligence play a part, saying AI is “less effective in factoring the unpredictable emotional and cultural factors that often shape successful strategy development and implementation.” Chief financial officer Fotis Chrysochos believes clients will continue to request consultants until AI reaches human levels of “compassion, empathy and behavioral understanding.”
Amy Lester, VA and VA mentor said that “even though AI can take some of the menial, repetitive work away, there will always be a requirement for human involvement to add humanity or personality.” David Rich, CEO, R Squared Group is questioning the ability of AI all together, saying that “half of what good consultants do is diagnose the problem by asking the right questions in the right order to the right audience,” a task that he said “would require very strong prompt engineering from the user of AI to determine all the factors.”
HYPPA Coach founder and ADHD consultant Mark Cann, who has built an AI focus coach, believes “a human consultant is more likely than an AI (which may lack previous context) to call you out on your BS to help you make progress.” He can, however, see the benefit of combining AI with consultants, in that “the client gets more attention on their high priority problems, and wastes less money on collection and analysis of data, which a consultant can use AI to do."
“AI isn't here to replace us, but to work alongside us. It can't think on its own, it requires the human!” said coach and consultant Cadi Jordan, “shouting from the rooftops!” AI creator Anna Poplevina concurs, believing “consultants will adapt by incorporating AI into their work to quickly analyze data for better, personalized advice,” meaning “this change won't replace them but will make their expertise more valuable as they navigate and apply AI insights to meet clients' needs.”
Cofounder and CEO of Lately AI, Kate Bradley Chernis is adamant that AI will not replace consultants and has a strong case for why. “Sentient machine learning does not exist,” she said. “Robots cannot think for themselves. The symbiosis of AI needing humans and humans needing AI is a movie we've all seen before.”
AI creator Lucas Pimentel added a new dimension to the debate, explaining that “the expectations from clients will be higher,” which he said will mean “consultants who don't perform well will be replaced by AI, and those who can use AI to enhance their impact will be in more demand than they can even fathom.” Finally, Chernis’ closing words of wisdom ring true for all knowledge workers. “When we fight it, we stall. When we embrace it, we soar.”
What’s the midground? AI-powered consultants.
While it’s romantic to think that empathy, human connection and genuine interest are required for a consulting relationship to work, the only thing that matters is the results. Your dog can give you empathy and your friends can give you human connection. Your consultant needs to grow your business.
Even if AI won’t replace consultants in their entirety, it will eliminate the need for them to do admin and data processing. They can move their effort to the work only they can do, benefitting their clients in the process, who can now access high level human insights without superfluous entries on the bill.
If entrepreneurs can train an AI model to gather information, dig deep, push back, spot patterns, give advice and hold them accountable, would they prefer to engage with a human or a robot at a fraction of the cost? Great consultants versus great AI tools is a debate to be had when they reach a level of proficiency that is unequivocally better. Until then, consultants race their clients to make the best use of AI, each proving that their side of the argument will ultimately be correct.

title: The Hard Questions Business Leaders Need To Ask About Adopting AI
text:
Pretend you’re a race car driver. You’re gearing up for your next Grand Prix.
You’re good. Your car is great. But you know the other drivers are also good. And some of their cars might even be better than yours.
Now pretend that when you get to the racetrack, your race engineer offers you a set of special new tires. These tires, they say, will make your car go 25 percent faster. At that pace, you’ll blow away the competition.
Is there any reason not to take them?
In the real world of motorsport, there are rules around tires. That’s because, as every racer knows, a worse driver with a better set of tires can beat a world champion with crappy tires. Better tires can give you an unfair advantage.
On the face of it, this is the scenario in front of us as business leaders today when it comes to artificial intelligence.
AI tools are popping up everywhere. If your industry hasn’t already been offered a new set of AI tires, just wait a few more days; it’ll happen.
So, duh, put the new tires on. Right?
Instinctively, our rational self interest will say yes. We want to win the race. But here’s the thing: the first-order effect of putting on these tires (going faster) might be followed by a few second-order effects:
- We’ll have to drive differently now and be careful in new ways; a car taking a corner too fast will spin out—or flip over.
- We don’t know how quickly these new tires will burn out—or if they’ll generate additional heat that will break something else on our car.
- We could, in putting on these 25 percent faster tires, be too busy—and use up all of our resources—to take advantage of the set of 50 percent faster tires that come out moments later. When our competitors get those tires, they’ll kick our butts.
- And, if we’re thinking long-term, we don’t yet know if the way these tires are sourced—or the things that will result from their widespread use—will have a negative effect on the world. E.g. what if the rubber for these tires comes from trees that are key to some region that gets destabilized when they’re chopped down; the destabilization spreads into World War III, and soon all racing is canceled!
If we only think about the surface-level, immediate-term promise of the AI tools that show up at our doors, we may jump in the car too quickly and create unintended consequences.
For the past 10 or so years, I’ve been called in as a speaker on innovation and change at leadership offsites for companies who are embarking on new frontiers. And in the last year, I’ve seen a clear pattern in companies I’ve consulted: Whether we’re talking about a sales kickoff or an HR team meeting, every one of my clients last year has asked, “How can we adopt AI now?”
Most of them are worried about adopting AI too slowly. But what they should be worried about is implementing it hastily.
Last year, for example, AI writing generation tools popped up everywhere, and companies—seeing the immediate monetary benefit of firing writers—started using AI to blog and SEO their way to glory. And then 1) The content turned out to be, for the most part, mediocre, and often inaccurate; 2) Companies in regulated industries started getting into trouble; 3) Better tools came out (like co-pilot tools that help writers rather than write for them); and 4) “Enshittification” became the word of the year as bad content took over search results and social media.
Do we need to go through all that pain? And what if next time the consequences are worse than bad search results?
The point is not to say “no” to the new tires. It’s to be thoughtful about when and how to put them on.
As leaders, we’ve got the weight of everyone’s expectations on our shoulders. Our teams, our stakeholders, the press, the peanut gallery. So it makes sense that we are desperate to throw on new tires as soon as we see a chance to seize a quick win. But if we’re going to make sustainable progress in this new era where AI advancements are only going to come quicker, we need to ask ourselves some hard questions whenever The Shiny New Thing presents itself.
Chief among those questions are:
Q. What are the possible ripple effects of adopting this AI tool?
Ask yourself, and then what? And then what?
Q. How will our team need to work differently now?
If you keep doing things the same way you always have, your adoption of new technology might make things worse, not better. Changing the way we play the game is what innovation is all about.
Q. Who will be affected adversely by this?
Even if there is a “net gain” to adopting AI, there’s a good chance that in the short (or even long) run there will be specific people who see a “net loss.” That could become a problem for you—and more importantly, the human cost to your decisions should be something we all care about.
Q. Should we invest resources into this particular AI tool now, or wait for the next iteration?
It can be advantageous to learn from the first movers and speed past them with the second wave. (Check out Chapter 5 of my book Smartcuts for more on this.)
Q. What don’t we know yet about this technology?
You may not want to know about how the sausage is made, but as a leader you need to know what you don’t know.
As a CEO of a company myself—in the film industry, no less—I fret about AI every time someone sends me a link to a new tool that people are going crazy over.
Seems like it happens every week now.
I’ve concluded that in many cases, not adopting new AI technology will likely result in worse things than embracing it. But that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t do the calculation each time on whether the juice is worth the squeeze—or how best to squeeze it. Whether you’re a humanist or a utilitarian, it doesn’t make sense to react to every new thing with, “Let’s go all in!” or “Let’s boycott it!”
As with so many things in leadership, the wiser path is the one you think about hardest, not the one you rush toward fastest.

title: Nvidia faces stiff test on Wall Street this week after 'parabolic' stock rally
text:
When Nvidia reports fiscal fourth-quarter earnings after the market close Wednesday, it will do so as the world's third most valuable public company. Investors are giving the company little margin for error.
Nvidia's stock price has soared fivefold since the end of 2022, as demand has skyrocketed for its graphics processing units that sit at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia's chips, such as the H100, are used by AI developers to create cutting-edge models like the ones OpenAI used to develop ChatGPT.
The company's market cap climbed to about $1.8 trillion last week, surpassing Alphabet and Amazon and now trailing only Microsoft and Apple.
"NVDA's stock appreciation has been parabolic," analysts at Bank of America wrote in a report Thursday. They reiterated their buy rating and said, "We think one interpretation of this NVDA move is a mix of fear and greed and indiscriminate investor chase for all things AI."
The other megacap tech companies all reported quarterly results weeks ago. All eyes are now on Nvidia.
Analysts are expecting a startling 240% increase in revenue from a year earlier to $20.6 billion for the period ending Jan. 28, according to LSEG, formerly known as Refinitiv. For every new dollar of sales the company generates, it's squeezing out even more profit.
Net income likely surged more than sevenfold to $10.5 billion from $1.41 billion a year earlier. In the third quarter, Nvidia's gross margin jumped to 74% from 53.6% the prior year.
Outsize growth is expected in Nvidia's data center business, which includes its AI chips. Analysts project an almost fourfold increase in revenue on an annual basis to $17.06 billion, according to FactSet.
Wall Street will be listening closely to commentary from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for an indication of how long these stratospheric growth rates are expected to last. The company already reported 200% year-over-year growth in the third quarter, and analysts are expecting a similar rate of expansion in the first period of this year.
One potential concern is that many of Nvidia's GPU sales are going to big tech companies such as Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Google. Any or all of them could decide to slow AI hardware spending at some point if they're not seeing intended benefits.
"All four communicated plans to significantly increase investment in their AI infrastructure this year, which bodes very well for NVDA's fourth quarter results and 2024 Q1 guidance," wrote D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria in a note Thursday. He has a neutral rating on the stock with a $410 price target.
However, he warns that the long-term picture for demand from Nvidia's top customers could be more mixed.
"They referred to their purchasing as 'flexible' and 'demand driven,' implying they would scale it down if we got past the current hype cycle," Luria wrote. "While we do not believe we are there yet, we are seeing possible early signs."
Nvidia's gaming segment, which includes graphics cards for PCs and laptops and used to be the company's primary business, is also expected to grow, but at a more measured rate of 49% to $2.72 billion in revenue. Some of Nvidia's gaming cards are also used by small companies and researchers for AI.
Thomas O'Malley of Barclays said the report will be fairly simple to analyze.
"The [data center] GPU number will be the only key metric that matters along with commentary on broader market adoption," O'Malley, who has a neutral rating on the shares, wrote Friday. "Most conversations we have center on the sustainability of the current run-rate in [data center], which is approaching $100B per year."
Other analysts are focused on whether Nvidia has enough supply to meet short-term demand, in part because the company relies on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company for its chips. There's also budding anticipation regarding the company's newest top-end AI chip, called B100, which starts shipping this year.
"We are particularly excited about Nvidia's plans to launch the B100 later in 2024 and the X100 in 2025," wrote Melius Research analyst Ben Reitzes, who recommends buying the stock, in a report last week. "If the upgrade from the A100 to the H100 is any indication, the Total Cost of Ownership benefit for data center operators will be enticing enough to fuel the upgrade and make 2025 a growth year."

title: Council Post: Beyond The Hype: Decoding The Real Magic Of Generative AI
text:
Miles Ward is the CTO of SADA Systems, a leading Google Cloud Partner.
I get it: You're bombarded with headlines about generative AI—the next big thing, the game-changer, the magic wand that'll turn your business into a unicorn overnight.
But, in the real world, AI superpowers come with responsibility—and a hefty dose of "know your dependencies." Before you rush off to buy capes and tights, let's talk practicality. Think of it like that scene in Spider-Man where he first swings through the city. Sure, it's exhilarating, but imagine him forgetting to web-sling before launching himself off a skyscraper. Splat goes the would-be superhero.
That's why, with generative AI, we need to think critically about the consequences of our choices (some more obvious than others) before we go soaring off into the unknown.
The Superhero Powers Of Generative AI
Take those fancy meeting summary tools, for example. They're a real time-saver, sure, but what about your data quality? Are you hallucinating your notes? Do you have service-level agreements in place to handle data retention and residency requirements? And let's not forget security—because, let's be honest, the last thing you want is accidentally broadcasting confidential conversations to the entire internet.
Now, that's not to say I'm a superhero skeptic. In fact, I see the potential of generative AI everywhere. At my company, we're using it to tackle mountains of paperwork, the kind that makes accountants weep and mortgage applications disappear into a black hole. Imagine automatically crunching receipts, comparing loan documents and summarizing reports—all with AI precision. That's magic worth celebrating.
But the real game-changer is the collaboration, the back-and-forth between you and the AI. Picture this: you toss a dataset at a generative AI tool and say, "Make sense of this." Instead of getting a jumble of numbers, you get an SQL query crafted for your needs. Then, the data flows back, but it's not just numbers anymore. The tool translates it into plain English, tailored to your role—whether you're a developer digging for technical insights or an investor wanting the market pulse.
That's where the real magic happens—the seamless shift between the digital and the human, the complex and the comprehensible.
And it doesn't stop there. Imagine meetings automatically transcribed, key takeaways instantly surfaced and knowledge shared effortlessly across teams. That's not just efficiency, folks; that's a cultural shift. We're talking about unlocking the true value of conversations, building bridges between departments and fostering a collaborative utopia. OK, or maybe just getting a bit more done with a bit less fuss.
Why AI Requires Security And Agility
But let's talk security—the masked elephant in the generative AI room. While the potential of these models is vast, so too are the potential vulnerabilities. People are, well, people. Some with good intentions, some with less savory ones. And their creativity extends beyond generating stunning poems or summarizing reports; it can also be directed toward nefarious ends.
I've spent countless hours brainstorming "gnarly attacks" these models could be subjected to. We built a comprehensive list of security scenarios and vulnerabilities, but let's be honest: We're at the tip of the iceberg. The bad guys are always evolving, always innovating. And in this game, the creatives will win, at least sometimes. That's the nature of the innovation arms race.
But here's the good news: We're not powerless. It's not enough to build a proof-of-concept, sprinkle some best practices like fairy dust and call it a day. We need to be agile, adaptive and constantly evolving our defenses.
That's why I ask companies a critical question: "How fast can you change your software?" If your update cycle resembles a medieval manuscript approval process, riddled with superfluous reviews, approvals and lawyerly cuddles, you're in trouble. In the world of generative AI, security changes need to happen at warp speed, not a glacial pace.
It's a two-pronged approach: thinking deeply about potential attack vectors and empowering companies to implement countermeasures rapidly. It's a constant dance, a continuous game of chess against the creative minds on the other side. Never a dull moment in tech.
Embracing AI Magic The Right Way
As we embrace the magic of generative AI, let's not forget the shadows lurking behind its brilliance. Let's be vigilant, proactive and adaptable. Let's build systems that are secure by design, evolve at the pace of innovation and keep the bad guys scrambling for their virtual chess pieces. In the battle for AI security, agility is the ultimate superpower.
As we wield these language models, we need to be mindful of bias, ethics and the potential pitfalls of putting too much faith in AI's black box. After all, even Spider-Man had to deal with Venom, and we don't want our AI partners turning into corporate symbiotes.
So, let's ditch the hype and embrace the reality. Generative AI isn't about overnight revolutions; it's about incremental changes, strategic partnerships and understanding the nuances of the digital world. It's about bridging the gap between the ones and zeros and the everyday human experience. That's the real magic—not superpowers, but supercharged collaboration, supersmooth efficiency and a super-slick future where technology does not replace us but empowers us.
